result:
There is a moment, just before you sit down to write something, when the page is not yet a page. It is a field. A wide, flat, unmarked plain that stretches out in every direction, and the thought you need has not yet decided whether to land in the center of it or drift off toward the edges and disappear. You feel this field with your hands, almost, as though the surface of the paper or screen were a kind of soil, cool and undisturbed, waiting for something to break through.

And then the first sentence goes down, and the field becomes a path. You are walking. You do not know where you are going. You only know the direction of your feet. This is the part that has always confused me most about the act of making a thing: the first word is a small act of faith. You say it into the air and it becomes a fact, and the fact constrains the second word, and the second constrains the third, and by the fifth you are no longer the architect of what you are building. You are a traveler in a city you didn't design.

I've spent a long time thinking about doors, actually. Not the dramatic kind, not the one that swings open onto a cliff edge or a kingdom of glass. I mean the smaller door. The one in a hallway in a house you used to live in. The one you walked past so many times your body learned its shape the way it learned the shape of the stairs. You didn't look at it. You didn't think about it. You just pushed it with your shoulder every morning and every evening, the same push, the same small mechanical gesture, and it swung inward or outward depending on which way you were facing, and you never noticed the hinge because you were carrying coffee, or a book, or a coat that smelled like rain.

But doors in houses are a metaphor, and I keep coming back to them because the metaphor is so thin, so close to the actual wood and iron and the sound of a latch, that I can't tell where the thing ends and the idea begins. Maybe there is no clean boundary. Maybe every object is a door and every door is an object, and the meaning only appears when you step through. Or maybe the meaning was there the whole time, sitting on the other side, and the door was just the shape it took to let you find it.

Outside my window the sky is doing that thing where it's not quite rain and not quite not-rain. The clouds are low and gray and textured, like something was pressed into wet plaster and left there. There's a bird on the wire. It has been there for maybe ten minutes, and it has not moved, which is somehow more interesting than movement would be, because stillness in a living creature feels like a held breath, like a question that has been paused mid-sentence. The bird is round and small and entirely unbothered by the sky's indecision, and I envy it. Not because it's wise. Because it's not trying. It's just... there. Round. Warm. Slightly alert.

I think about the word "there." We use it so casually. I am there. She is not there. The book is on the table. There is a dog in the street. There it is. There. As if the mere existence of a point in space can be asserted as a thing, a small coin tossed into the air to land. But "there" is also a direction. There = over there. Come here = stop being over there. The word is the whole geography of human language compressed into three letters, and I find that strange and a little sad. We have a whole lexicon for distance, for proximity, for between, and then we also have this one flat little word that says *this is where the thing is* and we are supposed to be satisfied. We are supposed to look at the thing and go, yes, there, I have found it, and move on to whatever else needs finding.

But you don't always move on. Some of the times you look at a thing and "there" is not the end of the sentence. It's the middle of it. You stand in the hallway and you look at the door and you think: there it is, the one I used to push with my shoulder every morning for six years, and the thought goes somewhere deeper than nostalgia, because it isn't nostalgia exactly. Nostalgia is for the past tense, for the golden hour, for the thing that was beautiful and is gone. This is different. This is the present tense of absence. The door is still there. The wall is still there. The hallway is still there, and the shape of your shoulder where it used to press is still there, if shape can be remembered. I don't think it can. I think the body keeps its own private ledger and the shape is in there, untranslatable, a sentence in a language I can't read.

The bird has flown. The wire is empty now, and the sky has not made its decision. It is raining very softly, the kind of rain that doesn't really commit to anything, that just exists as a fine suggestion, a whisper of water in the air, and I can smell the particular green smell that comes up from the pavement when the first drops hit it, the smell of cold stone waking up. I press my face a little closer to the window. The glass fogs where my breath lands, a small cloud that I watch evaporate. I make it again. And again. Not because I need to. Because I can. Because the fog is a small, temporary house of my own making, a shape that exists only as long as I keep breathing into it, and then it goes, and the glass is clear again, and the world behind it is the same world, unchanged, whether I looked through a fog or through nothing.

And I think that's the whole point, maybe. Not that we make things. But that we make them for a few seconds, and then we let them go, and the world is the world behind the glass. The fog is not the world. The fog is the proof that we were there, breathing, for a moment, and then the world resumes its slow, indifferent, beautiful turning, and the rain keeps falling because nothing asks the rain to be anything but rain.

And I close the window. Not because I need to. Because I'm going to eat bread.
